item.title: With Trump Secretly Evacuated, Imperiled Air Force One Became a Flying Decoy
item.description:
The threat to Air Force One was seen as so dire that they sneaked President Trump off the jet in a catering container to keep him safe. But the same dire threat did not stop them from then sending Air Force One into the skies anyway with a planeful of government employees, reporters and military personnel serving as decoys.

If the Iranians really were trying to shoot down the presidential plane last month, as U.S. officials concluded at the time, then the subterfuge in Ankara, Turkey, that protected the president also may have made targets of dozens of other people who flew aboard the jet, some of them unaware that Mr. Trump was not actually with them because it was considered too dangerous.

The government has on rare occasions engaged in sleight of hand to safeguard presidents from possible jeopardy, particularly for journeys to hazardous locations, such as when George W. Bush or Barack Obama flew to Iraq during days of war or when Bill Clinton made a brief visit to Pakistan with its history of terrorism. The Trump team’s ruse in Ankara, however, stands out not only for its misdirection but also for the way it shifted the evident peril to others and was kept secret long after Mr. Trump was out of harm’s way.

“They just didn’t seem to give a second thought to anybody but the president and the few people who were with him,” said Joe Lockhart, who served as White House press secretary to Mr. Clinton during his 2000 trip to Islamabad, the Pakistani capital. “We went out of our way to make sure the maximum number of people, especially civilians, were protected and not human shields. They didn’t even think about it. And to me, that’s the big difference.”

But other veterans of risky White House trips said there were times that extreme measures were justified to protect the president. Joseph W. Hagin, who as a top adviser to Mr. Bush helped organize his war zone trips and later served as Mr. Trump’s deputy White House chief of staff in his first term, said he would not second-guess the decision in Ankara.

“I understand there is concern for those flying on what was assumed to be the primary aircraft,” Mr. Hagin said, “but when you go to work at the White House or travel with the president, you are accepting a not-insignificant degree of risk. Telling everyone what’s up in an operation like this would have obviously jeopardized the president’s safety.”

When Mr. Bush or Mr. Obama brought staff members and reporters with them to war zones, Mr. Hagin added, those were dangerous moments, too. “This was no different than the trips to Iraq and Afghanistan,” he said. “You add up all the risks and figure out the tactics that give you the safest option, regardless of whose toes get stepped on or feelings get hurt.”

The government officials and reporters who traveled with presidents to war zones, of course, knew they were doing so, while those left on Air Force One in Ankara last month were not told of the increased threat. Journalists traveling in the back of the plane were instructed while still on the ground to keep their window shades closed during the July 8 flight from Ankara to Britain, where Mr. Trump landed secretly in another military plane. The president was then sneaked back onto Air Force One so that he could disembark in front of cameras as if he had been onboard all along.

The secret switch in Ankara, first reported on Monday by The Washington Post and confirmed by The New York Times and other news outlets, was so remarkable that it sounded like something out of Hollywood. In fact, it defied even the imagination of Andrew W. Marlowe, who wrote the screenplay for the iconic 1997 thriller “Air Force One,” featuring Harrison Ford as a president whose plane is hijacked. Mulling it over on Tuesday, Mr. Marlowe said he was sure the Secret Service was doing what was necessary to keep the president safe. But he added that it did not make Mr. Trump look all that good.

“Now real life isn’t a movie, but given the circumstances, I’m not sure I could ever script a moment like that for a heroic main character,” Mr. Marlowe said. “If the threat were that great, it’s hard to imagine the audience rooting for any character who would trade his own safety by treating the remaining civilians onboard as potential sacrificial lambs, especially without their informed consent.”

The White House did not respond to a request for comment about the calculations that went into the decision or whether extra measures were taken to protect the plane from any threat even without Mr. Trump onboard.

The extraordinary deception underscored the sense of danger felt by Mr. Trump, who was grazed by a would-be assassin’s bullet while campaigning in Butler, Pa., in 2024 and targeted by another armed man at his Florida golf course later that year. During the Biden administration, officials said that Iranian elements were trying to kill Mr. Trump. As recently as Tuesday, the police were investigating a bomb threat at a McDonald’s in Ohio near the site of a planned visit by Mr. Trump later that evening.

The Secret Service and military units charged with the president’s safety typically use decoys to confuse possible attackers, although not involving civilians without their knowledge. When any president travels in a motorcade, there are usually two identical armored limousines or sport utility vehicles with identical Washington, D.C., license plates to make it hard to know which one he is in. When he flies by Marine One, there are often three or four identical green-and-white helicopters flying together.

“If there’s an attack on the motorcade, the secure package splits off and everyone else is on their own, from some WH staff to some military officials, all reporters and members of Congress,” Ari Fleischer, a White House press secretary for Mr. Bush, wrote on social media on Tuesday. “The safety of potus always comes first. We don’t complain. That’s the way it is.”

A president of the United States, or POTUS in government jargon, is at once the most visible and most protected official in the country. The White House over the years has become a virtual fortress, and Mr. Trump plans to expand the security perimeter with a new fence around Lafayette Square across the street from the mansion.

At the same time, a president by tradition always travels with a pool of journalists who record his every public movement and comment. Such constant coverage has been considered vital in the nuclear era when a crisis can confront a president at any moment. Journalists were with John F. Kennedy when he was shot in Dallas on Nov. 22, 1963, and they were with Mr. Bush when terrorists attacked the United States on Sept. 11, 2001.

When presidents have made war zone trips in recent years, the White House typically summoned a select number of news executives to the Situation Room or called journalists to clue them in and swear them to secrecy so at least a few could go along and report about the visits once it was safe. Mr. Bush and Mr. Obama both took reporters with them to Afghanistan and Iraq, as did Mr. Trump in his first term. President Joseph R. Biden Jr. took one news reporter and one news photographer with him on a secret nine-and-a-half-hour train trip into war-torn Ukraine.

When Mr. Clinton traveled to Pakistan, he too switched planes to avoid detection by possible attackers. He had been urged not to go because parts of the country were havens for terrorist groups, but since he was already going to India, he felt compelled to stop in Islamabad for a few hours.

The original security plan called for fooling the accompanying journalists into thinking that Mr. Clinton had boarded the same C-17 military jet that they were on, while he would secretly get onto a separate Air Force version of a Gulfstream known as a C-20. “My vehement protest was you can’t use the media as decoys,” he said. “And they came back with a plan that satisfied me.”

Instead, according to another veteran of that trip who spoke on the condition of anonymity to avoid professional repercussions, they had Mr. Clinton walk around the nose of the C-17 to the other side where three smaller unmarked planes were waiting. The journalists were not able to see which of the three he boarded, but they saw that he had not gotten on the C-17.

Unlike the Trump team in Ankara, the Clinton team informed at least one of the pool journalists in advance, Susan Page of USA Today, who recounted the episode on Tuesday. And the White House then publicly disclosed the details more broadly once Mr. Clinton was safely out of harm’s way. Mr. Trump’s team, by contrast, never disclosed what happened in Ankara until The Post broke the story.

“It’s totally understandable that the White House would want to compartmentalize a security operation like this,” said John F. Kirby, a retired Navy rear admiral who served as a top spokesman for the White House, the State Department and the Pentagon during the Obama and Biden administrations. “I don’t fault them for going to lengths to keep the president safe or in withholding specific threat intelligence.”

“But,” he added, “they also have an obligation for the safety and security of those traveling with the president. And when the risk of that travel is knowable — as it certainly was in this case — they have an obligation to at least provide the broad contours of it so that travelers can make informed decisions.”

Mr. Hagin disagreed. “My only criticism is that it leaked,” he said. “It is very, very hard to move the president covertly, and when you burn one of these tactics it’s unlikely you could get away with it again, which just makes it even harder the next time you need to do it. This wasn’t the first time and it won’t be the last that an operation like this is required, regardless who is president.”

item.title: Warehouse Blaze in Portland, Ore., Is Headache for City Over a Week Later
item.description:
More than a week after a fire tore through a 116-year-old building in Portland, Ore., what remains of the badly damaged warehouse is causing disruptions and frustrating city officials.

The old Centennial Mills building, a former flour mill, sits a half-mile from Portland’s Union Station and abuts railroad tracks. When it went up in flames on Aug. 2, every floor of the eight-story warehouse collapsed. The cause of the blaze remains under investigation.

“A safety perimeter has been set up around the site to keep the public away from the potential collapse zone,” Dan Douthit, a spokesman for the city of Portland, said in an email. He added that the fire had gutted the building.

The city ordered the building’s owner to demolish it by Aug. 14, but the need for specialized engineers and equipment has complicated those efforts. “The building is too dangerous for even our investigators to be near or inside it,” Lauren Johnson, the city’s fire chief, said at a news conference on Monday.

Amtrak train service between Portland and Seattle has been suspended since the fire. The building is near railway tracks and bounded by the Willamette River, and officials are worried that the rumbling of a passing train could shake the building enough to bring it down. A safety zone has been established around the building, and a nearby park has been closed.

But Union Pacific, a freight transportation company, resumed operations on Tuesday in a decision city officials called a “significant risk to health and safety.”

A spokeswoman for Union Pacific, Robynn Tysver, said in an email statement that the transportation company was operating, but with limits. Its trains are running on the track farthest from the structure and traveling under a voluntary speed limit. She said the company was in close contact with the city.

“Union Pacific recognizes the challenges presented by this incident,” Ms. Tysver said in the statement, “but, with no end date on when this long-abandoned property will be demolished, we must consider the disruption the closure of this critical rail corridor has on regional industries, small businesses, ports and consumer goods.”

According to local news reports, Union Pacific did say it would not ship hazardous cargo past the building until Aug. 21.

Portland officials are concerned that the building’s collapse could result in “death or serious injury to those on the train and damage to the surrounding property,” Raymond Lee, the city administrator, said at the Monday news conference.

“We know Portlanders want answers,” he said. “We’re committed to sharing information as it becomes available. But this remains both an active investigation and a dangerous site.”

Amtrak is offering shuttle bus service for some routes, for those who have train tickets, while other routes have been canceled entirely. Customers can rebook or request a full refund at no additional cost, Amtrak said.

The building contained asbestos and possibly other harmful toxins, according to a statement from three investigating agencies, and the city has advised residents on how to more safely clean up ash and debris. The debris from the demolition is another concern the city aims to address.

item.title: Darline Graham Advances to the Republican Senate Runoff in South Carolina
item.description:
Senator Darline Graham, the sister of the late Senator Lindsey Graham, advanced on Tuesday to the special Republican primary runoff for Senate in South Carolina, when she will face Representative Ralph Norman, a longtime hard-line conservative lawmaker, according to The Associated Press.

The matchup on Aug. 25 will offer a sharp contrast in experience, though few policy differences. Ms. Graham, who stepped in to complete her brother’s Senate term after he died last month, has offered little in the way of specifics about her positions, other than to back President Trump and the Republican Party line. Mr. Norman is a five-term congressman and vice-chairman of the ultraconservative House Freedom Caucus.

Ms. Graham did not win the special primary outright, despite having Mr. Trump’s endorsement — an outcome, as she said on Tuesday morning, that she expected in the crowded race. Mr. Norman and other more experienced Republicans ran knowing that Ms. Graham, 62, a longtime advocate for people with disabilities, had been largely unknown and untested as a political novice. As of Tuesday, she had been in office for 28 days.

“This is a very emotional night,” Ms. Graham told reporters gathered in Columbia, S.C., on Tuesday night, “because I’m usually standing out here celebrating with Lindsey. I know he’s looking down right now, smiling.”

She rejected criticism that she had effectively inherited the Senate seat, saying that her parents taught her and her brother “that you’re not given anything in life.”

“If you want something, you work for it,” she said, vowing to listen to Republicans on the ground over the next two weeks. “That’s how I’ve tried to live my life.”

She said she had thanked Mr. Trump and was “hopeful” that he would campaign for her, “but we’ll see.” Her family stood behind her in the small recording studio where she made her remarks, without any supporters on hand.

Mr. Norman made the runoff after running neck and neck with Representative Russell Fry, an up-and-coming young lawmaker aligned with Mr. Trump, as results trickled in Tuesday night. Mr. Fry, 41, a two-term congressman from the Myrtle Beach area, did well in South Carolina’s growing northeast. But Mr. Norman attracted strong support around the South Carolina suburbs of Charlotte, N.C., where he is from, and in the upstate region around Greenville, which is rich in Republican voters.

“We have got some socialist Democrats,” Mr. Norman told a gathering of about a hundred people on Tuesday night at a restaurant in Rock Hill, N.C. “This is the party that is intent on taking over this country.”

Mr. Norman said he might not have been the first or second choice of some voters but said he wanted to be their “next choice.” He pledged to run over the next two weeks on a message of faith, family and freedom.

“Let’s win this thing!” he told supporters.

For Mr. Norman, 73, the race revived a political career that had appeared to be drawing to a close after he gave up his House seat and came in third in the Republican primary for governor in June. He was perhaps better prepared than any other South Carolina Republican to run an unexpected Senate race on very short notice after Mr. Graham’s death, having just competed in a statewide contest that had given him strong name recognition.

Mr. Norman did not win Mr. Trump’s endorsement in either the governor’s race or the special Senate race, likely because he backed former Gov. Nikki Haley of South Carolina over Mr. Trump in the 2024 Republican presidential primary. But Mr. Trump’s endorsement in this year’s race for governor did not prove decisive: His first choice, Pamela Evette, the state’s lieutenant governor, made the runoff but then lost. She had faced criticism for relying so heavily on the president’s support that she appeared to campaign on little else.

South Carolina is a solidly red state, but its Republican voters have a long history of rejecting legacy candidates and bucking the party establishment. In Ms. Graham’s case, she has had to contend with her brother’s sometimes difficult relationship with the state’s MAGA voters. They viewed Mr. Graham with some skepticism over his hawkish foreign policy views, his past support for comprehensive immigration reform and his failure to initially back Mr. Trump, though the two men eventually became close.

Ms. Graham has tried to distance herself from some of her brother’s views, saying that she would focus on domestic policy. But she has carefully avoided interviews with reporters and spent much of the past few weeks in Washington voting in the Senate rather than introducing herself to voters.

Mr. Trump held a telephone rally for Ms. Graham ahead of the election on Monday night, saying she stepped up “with tremendous poise and conviction” after her older brother’s death.

“She looks so nice, but she’s actually tough and strong,” he said on the call.

Tiffany Tan contributed reporting from Rock Hill, S.C.

item.title: Defending ‘Defund,’ Ending Fireworks: El-Sayed Deleted Old Posts and Videos
item.description:
Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for Senate in Michigan, was a prolific commentator for years, pontificating about the political issues of the day on social media, YouTube and various podcasts.

But if you’re looking for some of his takes from years ago, you won’t find them on YouTube. CNN reported on Tuesday that he had deleted a number of videos and posts where he floated the idea of abandoning fireworks on Independence Day, suggested replacing the Second Amendment with the “right to have health care” and expressed support for the “defund the police” movement.

A review of online archives by The New York Times shows that Dr. El-Sayed has made at least 160 videos from his public YouTube page private, including every post that predated the announcement of his Senate bid in April 2025. He has also deleted numerous posts on X.

He did not wipe away everything.

In one podcast episode from 2023 that was not deleted, he drew a loose link between American football and Manifest Destiny, the trans-Atlantic slave trade and the United States’ history of “destroying Native Americans,” saying that they were “kind of echoed in the ethos” of the sport.

Republicans seized on the newly unearthed content to attack Dr. El-Sayed, who won the Democratic primary last week and is facing former Representative Mike Rogers in a November contest seen as crucial to control of the Senate.

“Defund ICE, defund the police, and now a call to ban fireworks,” Senator Tom Cotton, Republican of Arkansas, wrote on X. “You can’t make this up. The Democratic party has gone off the deep end.”

The videos were made private, which means they are effectively deleted for everyone except Dr. El-Sayed. Auto-generated transcripts, titles and descriptions, however, are available on the Internet Archive and Filmot, which catalogs unlisted videos on YouTube. Because the original videos are no longer available, The Times could not independently verify the accuracy of the transcripts, whose content Dr. El-Sayed’s campaign did not dispute.

Democratic politicians have retreated from some of the more outspokenly liberal positions they took around 2020. Francesca Hong, the front-runner in Wisconsin’s Democratic primary for governor, recently walked back a 2020 social media post calling for Thanksgiving to be canceled, and Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, a Democrat from New York, on Sunday distanced herself from her calls to “abolish the police” that year.

Dr. El-Sayed’s campaign acknowledged that his YouTube page “was updated to post exclusively campaign content” and suggested that he did not still hold all of the views expressed in the deleted posts.

“Abdul is the former captain of his high school football team, loves Michigan football on Saturdays, and celebrates the Fourth of July with fireworks like the next Michigander,” Roxie Richner, a spokeswoman for Dr. El-Sayed, said in a statement. “Cherry-picked comments from old podcasts don’t reflect his beliefs today.”

Dr. El-Sayed has been unabashed about his progressive views during his campaign, including his belief that Immigration and Customs Enforcement should be abolished. He has pivoted on policing, however.

In one deleted post from June 2020, Dr. El-Sayed called the police “standing armies we deploy against our own people.” In another from the same month, he wrote, “Most major US cities spend WAY TOO MUCH on police departments to police poverty & WAY TOO LITTLE on public schools, health departments, recreation departments, & housing to eliminate poverty.”

He added, “Fixing that is what the #Defund movement is about.”

Last month, he told CNN that he had deleted old social media posts about the “defund” movement because they were taken “out of context” for “clickbait.” And on Tuesday, Dr. El-Sayed’s campaign said that he now believed that funding for law enforcement recruitment, retention and retirement should improve, but that he also supported investing in community programs and other ways to reduce violence.

In one deleted video from April 2023, Dr. El-Sayed opined that the “right to bear arms” was not about allowing people to carry guns, but instead “about being able to sponsor a militia at the state level to protect against tyranny from the federal government.” On Tuesday, Ms. Richner, his campaign spokeswoman, said that Dr. El-Sayed “respects the Second Amendment, and also believes that access to health care is a right.”

In a now-deleted July 2024 video, Dr. El-Sayed suggested that Americans should consider alternatives to fireworks on Independence Day, writing in the video’s description that Detroit experienced “the worst air quality in the entire world” after July 4. “Fireworks just aren’t worth it,” read the title of one section, while another pointed out that they could trigger post-traumatic stress disorder in veterans and pose risks to children and pets.

His campaign pointed to an X post from July 2025 to show how Dr. El-Sayed’s views had evolved.

“Happy Fourth of July, Michigan!” he wrote. “Enjoy the fireworks as we commit ourselves to building a country where all of us can thrive.”

item.title: Trump Says Secret Service Ordered Air Force One Swap
item.description:
President Trump said on Tuesday evening that the Secret Service and the military decided he would take a secret flight out of Turkey last month while his staffers and the traveling press flew on a decoy Air Force One.

“It’s only up to Secret Service,” Mr. Trump told reporters after landing in Washington following his trip to Ohio, in his first public comments about the evacuation from Turkey. “I just follow what they like to do. So I go by Secret Service and the military. They wanted me to go in a different flight, a different plane, equal safety but they wanted me to do it. So I do it.”

Mr. Trump’s effort to redirect questions to his protective detail and military advisers came as his administration faced increasing scrutiny over the revelation that Mr. Trump was secretly evacuated out of Turkey on a military jet after the NATO summit last month amid threats against him from Iran.

Despite Mr. Trump and other officials saying publicly last month that he would leave Turkey on one of the older versions of Air Force One rather than a luxury 747-8 donated by Qatar that he had flown in on, his officials had decided instead to sneak him into a military jet via a catering container.

The original plane, however, still carried White House staffers and top officials including Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, along with Stephen Miller, the president’s top domestic policy adviser, and Steven Cheung, the White House communications director.

Mr. Trump on Tuesday night framed the decision as one that was out of his control. “I get a lot of threats,” Mr. Trump said when asked why the Secret Service moved him to a different plane.

“I just have to do what they say,” he added. “They go for safety and I have to do what they say.”

The Secret Service usually works with intelligence officials, the State Department and the military when planning on how to respond to threats against the president overseas, according to former homeland security officials.

Agents in the Secret Service have generally lived by the ethos of bringing the president where he wants to go, even if it means putting their bodies on the line. And Mr. Trump has in the past shown that he has a strong say in the decision-making process over risky movements.

In 2020, while being treated for Covid-19, a masked Mr. Trump took a break from the hospital to drive by well-wishers inside a hermetically sealed, armored Chevy Suburban with at least two Secret Service agents. He also continued to campaign while the pandemic spread, causing some Secret Service agents to privately question whether additional precautions would be put in place to protect the detail.

When asked on Tuesday evening why it was too dangerous for Mr. Trump to fly on Air Force One from Turkey but not too dangerous to evacuate the press, Mr. Trump claimed without providing evidence that the secret plane was actually at “greater risk.”

The plane that the public did not know he was on, rather than the plane carrying his staffers and Air Force One insignia, was the plane they were “more likely to go for,” he said.

item.title: Peggy Flanagan, a Progressive, Wins the Democratic Senate Primary in Minnesota
item.description:
Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan won the Democratic primary race for Senate in Minnesota on Tuesday, according to The Associated Press, defeating a centrist congresswoman in the latest victory for the party’s left wing.

Ms. Flanagan, 46, campaigned as an anti-establishment fighter, calling for universal health care and a higher federal minimum wage. She prevailed over Representative Angie Craig, a moderate Democrat from a swing district, leading by nearly 20 percentage points with more than 95 percent of votes counted.

In her victory speech, Ms. Flanagan signaled that she would focus on the rising cost of living in the general election, and reveled in winning a primary in which she had been heavily outspent by Ms. Craig.

“For months now, I have been telling you that this campaign was about the many versus the money,” she said. “Well, guess what, the many just won.”

Ms. Craig, for her part, said she had called Ms. Flanagan to concede. “Peggy’s story is one of grit, of determination and resolve,” Ms. Craig said in a speech late Tuesday, adding, “To every person that supported me, I ask you tonight to support and elect Peggy Flanagan.”

The Minnesota primary was shaped by a backlash to the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown in the state last winter. Ms. Flanagan criticized Ms. Craig over a vote she made for one of Mr. Trump’s signature immigration policies — a move that the congresswoman said she had come to regret.

Ms. Flanagan, a member of the White Earth Band of Ojibwe, could become the first Native American woman to serve in the Senate if she wins the November general election.

She will face Michele Tafoya, a moderate Republican and a former N.F.L. sideline reporter, in a Democratic-leaning state that has sometimes sent Republicans to Washington in recent decades. Former Vice President Kamala Harris, whose running mate was Gov. Tim Walz of Minnesota, won the state by only four percentage points in the 2024 presidential election.

The winner of the Senate race will succeed Tina Smith, a Democrat, who is retiring.

Ms. Flanagan has said she plans to tie Ms. Tafoya to Mr. Trump, saying her Republican rival would be a “‘Yes Sir, Mr. President’ Senator.” Even before Tuesday, Ms. Tafoya, who was not endorsed by Mr. Trump, had begun to focus on Ms. Flanagan, casting her as a career politician and attacking her over a major fraud scandal in the state government’s social safety net programs.

Ms. Flanagan’s candidacy will offer another general-election test case of the left’s ability to win in competitive terrain. Her victory on Tuesday came a week after Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, a progressive former public health official, captured the Democratic nomination for Senate in Michigan, a pivotal swing state.

And it ended a bruising Democratic race in Minnesota. Ms. Craig argued that Ms. Flanagan had unique weaknesses as a general-election candidate, citing the fraud scandal.

Ms. Flanagan criticized Ms. Craig for accepting financial support from corporate and industry groups, including some with undisclosed donors.

Ms. Flanagan was backed by left-wing leaders including Senators Bernie Sanders of Vermont and Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts. Locally, she was backed by Senator Smith and Representative Ilhan Omar, a progressive from Minneapolis.

Ms. Craig, who raised significantly more money than Ms. Flanagan, drew the support of establishment figures including Representative Hakeem Jeffries of New York, the Democratic House leader, and Representative Nancy Pelosi of California, the former speaker.

Senator Chuck Schumer of New York, the leader of Senate Democrats, did not publicly back a candidate.

Governor Walz, who was once mentored by Ms. Flanagan but has had a sometimes tense relationship with her in recent years, also stayed neutral. But his wife, Gwen Walz, endorsed Ms. Craig.

“We’ll all be on the same team come Wednesday morning,” Ms. Flanagan said in an interview on the eve of Primary Day.

Ernesto Londoño contributed reporting.

item.title: 5 Things to Know About David Crowley, the Democratic Candidate for Wisconsin Governor
item.description:
David Crowley, the Milwaukee County executive and a moderate Democrat, won the Democratic nomination for governor of Wisconsin early Wednesday, upsetting a democratic socialist who had held a significant lead in opinion polls.

Mr. Crowley had dropped out of the race last month, only to jump back in 10 days later and accept an endorsement from Gov. Tony Evers after another leading candidate ended her campaign. Still, Mr. Crowley received far less attention in the race because of the energy that Francesca Hong, the democratic socialist candidate, appeared to be generating from a motivated progressive base.

Here are five things to know about him:

1. He trailed far behind in limited opinion polls of the primary race. Mr. Crowley had been seen as a long-shot candidate going into Tuesday, with Ms. Hong widely seen as the front-runner.

But she also attracted challenging headlines over past comments she had made criticizing holidays including Thanksgiving and Halloween. Prominent progressives including Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York and Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont declined to endorse her. And many Democrats worried that she would not be a competitive general-election candidate in a battleground state.

Mr. Crowley capitalized on Ms. Hong’s struggles, casting himself in the final days of the race as a choice with bipartisan appeal.

His campaign manager, Garren Randolph, said in a statement early Wednesday that Mr. Crowley was now “focused on bringing people together, earning the support of Democrats, Republicans, Independents, and anyone who believes Wisconsin is at its best when we work together and deliver results.”

2. His endorsement from Mr. Evers played a key role. Mr. Crowley found an important late-race champion in the departing Democratic governor, whose decision not to run for a third term set the stage for the contest. Mr. Evers argued that Mr. Crowley would be a strong general-election candidate and that his background leading Wisconsin’s largest county would prepare him for the job of governor.

“He gets stuff done,” Mr. Evers said at one event, adding: “He is an administrator. He is an executive. And he’s got a heart as big as they come.”

3. He would be Wisconsin’s first Black governor. Mr. Crowley has already broken some barriers in Wisconsin. He is the first Black Milwaukee County executive. Now 40, he also became the youngest person to serve in the role when he took the post six years ago.

4. He has said he was evicted three times as a child. Mr. Crowley, who grew up on Milwaukee’s North Side, has leaned into his personal history. Both of his parents struggled with addiction and mental health challenges, according to his campaign. He has said his childhood inspired him to become a community organizer and later a state lawmaker. Even as a child, his family nicknamed him Governor, he has said.

“I wanted to feed my aunt, my grandmother, my uncles, take out the garbage and do the dishes,” he told The Capital Times of Madison. “I wanted to serve my family before I actually sat down and started eating. And so they used to call me ‘Governor.’”

5. He is cautious about proposing tax increases. Mr. Crowley has positioned himself as a moderate on taxes, expressing concern about raising them on the wealthy and calling for a “holistic” review of the tax system.

“We absolutely need to tax the ultrawealthy,” he said at a candidates’ debate last month. “But we need to be smart about how we’re doing things long-term.” And in a post on social media last month about property taxes, he wrote, “The taxes are too damn high.”

item.title: 8 Takeaways From Tuesday’s Primaries
item.description:
An agonizingly close race in the Democratic primary for governor of Wisconsin ended with an upset win for the moderate David Crowley early on Wednesday, the latest turn in a rancorous battle between the party’s ascendant left and its old guard that has defined primary season this year.

Mr. Crowley, the Milwaukee County executive and standard-bearer for moderates in the race, vastly exceeded expectations by defeating State Representative Francesca Hong, a democratic socialist who built a supercharged campaign of energized supporters and overwhelmingly led in most public polls.

Other races were called before midnight. Here are eight takeaways from Tuesday’s long night.

For weeks, polls established Ms. Hong, a democratic socialist, as the clear front-runner. But Mr. Crowley outperformed expectations on Tuesday, narrowly edging his left-wing rival.

Soon after polls closed on Tuesday night, it became clear that, for the second consecutive week in a Democratic primary, a democratic socialist was not winning by as big a margin as predicted. Last week in the Democratic Senate race in Michigan, Dr. Abdul El-Sayed defeated Representative Haley Stevens in a closer-than-expected contest that was not called until the next morning.

But in Wisconsin, the wait was shorter. And the outcome was far different for the progressive movement.

Ms. Hong was the subject of a string of bad headlines in the final days of the campaign, including some over past remarks she made online. Those comments included her derision of Thanksgiving and other holidays, which she walked back.

The negative publicity could have been a bridge too far for some voters, especially if they made their choices in the final days of the campaign. In addition, some of the biggest national names in progressive politics, including Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont and Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York, sat out the race.

Ms. Hong spent more time campaigning in rural Wisconsin than any other candidate, and it appeared to pay off, given how well she was doing in those parts of the state. Democratic socialists and other progressives have won a string of races on the strength of their ground games and populist left-wing proposals that are resonating with many voters. The old-fashioned takeaway? Showing up in person to make your case makes a difference.

But in Ms. Hong’s race, that wasn’t enough.

In another Midwestern race in neighboring Minnesota, the progressive lieutenant governor, Peggy Flanagan, won the Democratic nomination for Senate, notching a victory for the party’s left wing. Ms. Flanagan’s victory over Representative Angie Craig, who had far more financial resources, was a triumph for what some saw as a more palatable form of progressivism.

Ms. Flanagan ran on a suite of progressive priorities — calling for universal health care, a higher federal minimum wage and an end to unconditional U.S. aid for Israel. She said she would challenge the Democratic establishment in Washington.

But Ms. Flanagan did not describe herself as a democratic socialist, and she captured support from a broader constellation of Democrats and progressives, including Mr. Sanders and Senators Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts, Christopher S. Murphy of Connecticut and Tina Smith of Minnesota, whose retirement opened the seat. Ms. Flanagan also did not suffer from a social-media footprint denigrating Thanksgiving. She will face Michele Tafoya, a Republican and former sports broadcaster, in November.

On the Republican side, Senator Darline Graham, a political newcomer and President Trump’s choice to succeed her brother, the late Senator Lindsey Graham, advanced to a runoff alongside Representative Ralph Norman, a hard-line conservative and a leader of the House Freedom Caucus.

Ms. Graham’s triumph over a field of more experienced candidates provided yet another show of the power that Mr. Trump holds over Republicans. The president came around to the idea that Ms. Graham should run for the seat after she was tapped to finish her brother’s term and met with the president in the Oval Office. He made very clear that he admired her poise.

Ms. Graham had been in the Senate 28 days as of Tuesday, exactly one month after Mr. Graham died. In her remarks on election night, she displayed a steady countenance. She talked up Mr. Trump’s domestic agenda while also touting that she passed a bill sanctioning Russia that would have make her hawkish brother proud.

And she let voters in on her grief, saying she has not had a lot of time to process his death.

“I think a lot about what I would say to him, what he would say,” she said. “Right now, I think he would be very proud.”

Mr. Norman, a five-term congressman, had given up his House seat and come in third in the Republican primary for governor in June. His political career appeared to be over.

But running a statewide campaign, even a losing one, gave Mr. Norman the name recognition and organization to jump into the mad dash of a special Senate primary election after Mr. Graham died last month. And that’s what Mr. Norman did, coalescing enough conservative support around South Carolina to advance to the runoff against Ms. Graham.

His advancement also gave Ms. Graham bragging rights as the lone Trump-supported candidate in the race. Although Mr. Norman is seen as a hard-line conservative, his support for Nikki Haley in the 2024 presidential contest may have cost him the president’s affections.

Ms. Graham said on Tuesday that she is “hopeful” that Mr. Trump will campaign for her in the runoff, “but we’ll see.”

Representative John Larson, a 78-year-old Democrat seeking a 15th term in office, lost his primary race in Connecticut’s First Congressional District to Luke Bronin, former mayor of Hartford, in the latest example of restive Democratic voters ousting older lawmakers.

Mr. Bronin, a 47-year-old former Navy intelligence officer, campaigned explicitly on generational change. His victory followed wins by younger challengers in congressional contests in New York and Denver.

Those races pitted younger progressives against older moderates, while the Connecticut race was largely centered on age. Mr. Larson suffered a complex partial seizure on the House floor last year.

Remember Mike Lindell? He lost.

Tim Balk, Julie Bosman, Lisa Lerer and Ernesto Londoño contributed reporting.

item.title: Center-Left Candidate Defeats Democratic Socialist in Wisconsin’s Governor Primary
item.description:
David Crowley, the Milwaukee County executive, won the Democratic nomination for governor in Wisconsin, according to The Associated Press. His stunning upset sets up a showdown with Representative Tom Tiffany of Wisconsin, a Republican with close ties to President Trump who easily won his party’s primary.

A surprise surge in the final days of the race helped Mr. Crowley narrowly defeat Francesca Hong, a chef, state lawmaker and democratic socialist who had held a commanding lead in the polls for months. Gov. Tony Evers, a Democrat, endorsed Mr. Crowley, who out-raised Ms. Hong in July with the embrace of the more centrist Democratic establishment, and joined him on the campaign trail, warning Democratic voters that Ms. Hong would likely lose to Mr. Tiffany.

The win was all the more remarkable because Mr. Crowley had dropped out of the race in early July as his support and campaign funds dwindled. He only jumped back in 10 days later to accept Mr. Evers’ endorsement, saying that he and his wife had prayed and arrived at the decision to return. Mr. Evers told Democratic primary voters that Mr. Crowley was the candidate most likely to beat Mr. Tiffany in November.

“We are seeing an incredible shift of momentum,” Mr. Crowley said last week.

During his campaign, Mr. Crowley promised that if elected, he would push to build more housing in Wisconsin, improve the health care system and raise Wisconsin’s minimum wage to $20 an hour by 2030, from the current $7.25.

He faced Ms. Hong; Sara Rodriguez, the state’s lieutenant governor; Mandela Barnes, a former lieutenant governor; Kelda Roys, a state lawmaker; and Joel Brennan, a former state cabinet member.

A Marquette University Law School poll released last month showed Ms. Hong leading the field with 38 percent of the vote, Mr. Barnes with 16 percent and Mr. Crowley with seven percent.

But that field steadily imploded. In the final weeks before the primary, Ms. Rodriguez ended her campaign when she discovered financial mismanagement.

Perhaps the best-known candidate in the race at the time, Mr. Barnes, abruptly suspended his campaign in late July, saying in a message to supporters that it was time to focus on beating Mr. Tiffany.

Mr. Tiffany, 68, grew up on a farm, worked as a dam tender and now represents a conservative-leaning district in western Wisconsin. He has said that his priorities as governor will be to lower taxes, bring transparency to health care and protect farmland in Wisconsin.

Mr. Trump declared in his endorsement of Mr. Tiffany that the congressman has “always been at my side.” As the primary drew near, Mr. Tiffany presented himself as a bulwark against “big-government socialism,” saying that his opponents wanted to empty prisons and abolish the police. He was the only major candidate on the Republican ballot.

“We’re going to paint that clear contrast every single day between the craziness of the left and the common sense that we’re going to bring to Madison,” Mr. Tiffany said at a recent campaign stop.

item.title: After a Typo, Officers Used Excessive Force in an Arrest, a Report Finds
item.description:
Two San Francisco police officers thought they had spotted a stolen car one night in July 2024. After stopping the vehicle, they smashed in a window, dragged out the driver and then tackled, pepper sprayed and handcuffed him. They had the wrong man.

The officers had typed the car’s license plate number incorrectly into their patrol car’s computer system.

A city agency that investigates complaints against the police said on Tuesday that the officers had used “excessive force” during the mistaken arrest of Matthew Ludwig, the driver. They violated multiple policies, the agency said in a report, including spraying him at close range and drawing a firearm without cause.

Despite the case of mistaken identity, prosecutors spent over a year seeking to convict Mr. Ludwig for reckless driving and resisting arrest. Fourteen months after the traffic stop, he was found dead in Kentucky, of an apparent suicide.

“Nothing justifies the amount of violence that S.F.P.D. officers used on Mr. Ludwig, especially when it stemmed from their own mistake,” Brian Cox, who leads the integrity unit of the San Francisco public defender’s office, said in a statement on Tuesday.

While representing Mr. Ludwig against the charges, the defender’s office filed the complaint resulting in the investigation by the city watchdog agency, the San Francisco Department of Police Accountability.

The district attorney’s office, which prosecuted Mr. Ludwig, did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Tuesday. The San Francisco Police Department said it could not comment “due to pending litigation” and referred questions to the city attorney’s office, which said it had not been served a lawsuit on the matter.

It was unclear if the two officers, identified in the complaint as Jonathan Zepeda and Vinesh Govindbhai, had legal representation. Efforts to reach the officers on Tuesday were also unsuccessful.

Based on its findings, the watchdog agency will make a recommendation on disciplining the officers to either the San Francisco Police Department or the San Francisco Police Commission, the latter of which can terminate or decertify officers, Mr. Cox said.

Those recommendations are not made public. The discipline process can be lengthy because officers in California receive significant employment protections.

According to the complaint filed by the public defender’s office, the two officers spotted a Honda Accord late on July 4, 2024, that they believed to be stolen and pursued the driver. Officer Zepeda later said he had observed the car from a distance “running multiple red lights,” according to the complaint.

A few blocks away, Mr. Ludwig stopped behind several cars at a red light. The officers stopped behind him and got out of their car, but did not recheck the license plate, activate their patrol lights, order Mr. Ludwig to pull over or check if his door was unlocked, according to the complaint.

Body-camera footage shows one of the officers, identified in the complaint as Officer Govindbhai, smashing the driver’s-side window with a baton before dragging Mr. Ludwig from the car by the hood of his sweatshirt, pinning him to the ground and bashing his head into the pavement.

Before being forced into handcuffs, Mr. Ludwig can be heard on the video shouting, “I wasn’t doing nothing, bro.” An officer then sprayed him at very close range, directly into his eyes. A short time later, Mr. Ludwig can be heard wheezing and telling the officers repeatedly that he cannot breathe.

“This case shows how easily police can wrongfully target someone,” Mr. Cox said.

According to the complaint, the officers realized only after Mr. Ludwig was handcuffed that they had entered the license plate number incorrectly. But they proceeded to arrest him anyway.

The public defender’s officer said that Mr. Ludwig could not afford the impound fee necessary to recover his car and that the city had sold it at auction. Prosecutors then charged him with reckless driving and resisting arrest.

In September 2025, while charges against him were pending, Mr. Ludwig was found dead at a park in Morehead, Ky., according to the local police. He was 47.

Brandon Coleman, a deputy public defender who represented Mr. Ludwig, said in a statement that as a result of the arrest, his client had “lost virtually everything that he owned,” including his car and a recreational vehicle that he had shared with his girlfriend, which was towed a few days after the encounter.

Before his death, prosecutors had offered Mr. Ludwig’s lawyer the opportunity for him to avoid a criminal conviction if he would take responsibility for his actions.

“But Ludwig hadn’t done anything wrong,” the public defender’s office said.
